lessonGoal: Students will read an informational text about how ancient Greeks explained personality, identify the main idea and supporting details, learn psychology and classification vocabulary, and write short explanatory responses about personality types and human behavior.

warmUp.title: Warm-up
warmUp.instructions: Think about personality and human behavior. Answer the warm-up questions below. There are no right or wrong answers.
questions: How would you describe your personality in three words?
Why do people like personality tests or quizzes?
Do you think personality can be explained easily? Why or why not?

article.title: How Ancient Greeks Explained Personality
article.source: Source: Adapted from teacher-provided classroom source image.
paragraphs: Thousands of years ago, long before modern psychology existed, people wanted to understand why human beings behave in different ways. According to ancient Greek doctors, human mood and personality depended on the balance of four body fluids: yellow bile, black bile, phlegm, and blood. These four fluids were known as the 'four humours.' Medical thinkers believed that a healthy person had a perfect balance of all four humours. However, if one fluid became dominant, it was believed to change a person’s temperament, mood, and emotional state.

Each of the four humours was linked to a specific personality type. For example, too much yellow bile was believed to make a person irritable, short-tempered, and stubborn. On the other hand, an excess of blood was believed to make a person cheerful, energetic, and optimistic. Meanwhile, too much phlegm made someone calm and passive, while an excess of black bile was associated with a gloomy or anxious nature. This early theory helped people explain why someone might be calm, gloomy, outgoing, or anxious long before scientific psychology was developed.

Even though the four humours theory was not scientifically true, the idea remained popular for a very long time. For over two thousand years—continuing through the Middle Ages and into the time of William Shakespeare—doctors, writers, and ordinary people used the humours to describe human character. Even though modern science eventually proved that body fluids do not determine personality, the theory survived for centuries because it provided a clear structure to organize and explain human behavior when no other medical knowledge existed.

Some echoes of this ancient idea still appear today in modern culture and psychology. Although we no longer blame body fluids for our moods, people remain deeply interested in personality classification. Modern personality tests, such as the Myers-Briggs test, still group people into traits like 'extroverted' or 'calm.' One media psychology expert explained that classification is our built-in mechanism for organizing information. In other words, humans naturally like to group complex ideas and people into categories. The four humours theory may be unscientific, but our desire to classify personality remains as strong today as it was in ancient Greece.

mainIdeaQuestion.title: Main Idea
mainIdeaQuestion.question: What is the main idea of the article?
options: A. Ancient Greeks correctly proved that personality comes from body fluids.
B. Ancient Greeks used the four humours to explain personality, and people still like classifying personality today.
C. Shakespeare invented the four humours theory.
D. Modern psychology says personality tests are always scientifically perfect.
mainIdeaQuestion.explanation: The article explains that ancient Greeks believed personality depended on four humours, and although this theory was not scientifically true, people today still use personality categories and tests to understand behavior.

questions.question: What were the 'four humours' according to ancient Greek doctors?
options: A. Four types of brain cells used in modern psychology
B. Four body fluids believed to control mood and personality

questions.explanation: According to ancient Greek doctors, the four humours were four body fluids (yellow bile, black bile, phlegm, and blood) that controlled mood and personality.

questions.question: Why was the four humours theory NOT the same as modern scientific psychology?
options: A. It was not scientifically true, but it gave people a structure to explain behavior before modern science existed.
B. It relied entirely on modern computer algorithms and data analysis.

D. It was created recently by media experts.
questions.explanation: The article explains that the four humours theory was not scientifically true, but people used it because modern scientific psychology did not exist yet.

options: A. Because modern personality tests measure body fluids like blood and phlegm.
B. Because humans have a built-in mechanism for organizing information into categories.

questions.explanation: The article explains that classification is our built-in mechanism for organizing information, so both ancient humours and modern tests fulfill the human desire to classify personality.

languageFocus.title: Language Focus
languageFocus.explanation: In informational and explanatory texts, writers use specific linking expressions to state sources (according to), explain historical beliefs (was believed to, was linked to, depended on), provide examples (for example), show contrast (even though), and link past ideas to present habits (today, we still).
examples: According to ancient Greek doctors, personality depended on body fluids.
Too much yellow bile was believed to make a person irritable and stubborn.
Too much blood was linked to a cheerful and energetic personality.
Even though this theory was not scientifically true, it remained popular for centuries.
Today, we still use personality tests to classify human behavior.
practice: Complete the sentence: According to the ancient Greek theory, personality depended on __________.
Write one sentence using 'was believed to' to explain how body fluids affected mood.
Write one sentence using 'even though' to contrast ancient humours with modern science.
Write one sentence using 'today, we still' to connect past theories with modern personality tests.

writingPractice.title: Writing Practice
writingPractice.description: Write short responses to the questions below. Use 2–4 complete sentences for each response.

prompts.question: Why did ancient Greeks use the four humours to explain personality?
prompts.modelAnswer: Ancient Greeks used the four humours to explain personality because modern psychological science did not exist yet. They believed that four body fluids—yellow bile, black bile, phlegm, and blood—controlled human mood and temperament. Balancing these fluids gave them a simple way to understand different human behaviors.
prompts.compareTip: Did your answer explain that ancient Greeks lacked modern psychology and believed body fluids controlled mood and behavior?

prompts.question: Why was the four humours theory different from modern psychology?
prompts.modelAnswer: The four humours theory was different from modern psychology because it was not scientifically true. Ancient doctors incorrectly believed that physical body fluids determined emotional temperaments. In contrast, modern psychology uses scientific evidence, brain studies, and behavioral research to analyze personality.
prompts.compareTip: Did your answer contrast unscientific beliefs about body fluids with modern scientific psychology?

prompts.question: Why do people still enjoy personality tests today?
prompts.modelAnswer: People still enjoy personality tests today because humans have a built-in mechanism for organizing information into categories. Modern quizzes like the Myers-Briggs test offer simple labels like 'extroverted' or 'calm' to help people describe themselves. It fulfills our natural desire to understand ourselves and others.
prompts.compareTip: Did your answer mention the human desire to classify information or mention personality tests like Myers-Briggs?

prompts.question: Do you think classifying personality is useful or too simple? Explain your answer.
prompts.modelAnswer: I think classifying personality can be useful as a starting point, but it becomes too simple if used too strictly. Personality categories help people communicate basic traits like being outgoing or quiet. However, human behavior is very complex, so we should not limit anyone to a single label.
prompts.compareTip: Did you state your opinion clearly and explain both the benefits and limitations of classifying personality?

writingTask.title: Writing Task
writingTask.prompt: Write a short explanatory paragraph of 100–140 words answering this question: Why do people try to classify personality, and is this useful?
checklist: Explain the ancient Greek four humours theory.
Give at least two reasons why people classify personality.
Use at least one detail from the article.
Use classification or explanation language such as according to, was believed to, for example, even though, or today we still.
End with a clear concluding sentence.
writingTask.modelAnswer: People try to classify personality because it helps them understand human behavior more easily. According to the ancient Greek theory, personality depended on the balance of four humours: yellow bile, black bile, phlegm, and blood. For example, too much yellow bile was believed to make a person irritable, while too much blood was believed to make someone cheerful. Even though this theory was not scientifically true, it helped people organize different moods and behaviors. Today, people still enjoy personality tests because they want simple ways to describe themselves and others. However, personality is very complex, so categories should not be used too strictly. Overall, personality classification can be useful, but it should be seen as a starting point, not a perfect answer.

rubric.excellent: Clearly states an opinion on personality classification, explains the ancient Greek four humours theory, and provides at least two well-reasoned explanations for why humans classify behavior.
rubric.developing: States an opinion, but the explanation of the four humours or reasons for classification are incomplete or vague.
rubric.beginning: Opinion is unclear and fails to explain why people classify personality.

rubric.developing: Uses some target language, but with minor grammatical or connector errors.

teacherNotes: Explain clearly that the four humours theory is historical, not modern science.
Help students understand that old theories can still influence language and culture.
Use simple examples of personality words: calm, cheerful, anxious, outgoing, gloomy.
Encourage students to support written answers with details from the article.
For lower-level students, provide sentence frames.
For stronger students, ask them to compare ancient classification with modern personality tests.

teachingScript.actions: Welcome students and write 'PERSONALITY' on the board. Ask students to share three words that describe their personality. Introduce the idea that humans have tried to explain personality for thousands of years. Ask: Why do people like taking online personality quizzes or tests like Myers-Briggs? Encourage student pairs to discuss initial ideas before sharing with the class.

Pre-teach key terms: personality, mood, humour, balance, irritable, cheerful, gloomy, extroverted, classification. Clarify that in historical medicine, 'humour' referred to body fluids, not jokes or comedy. Model pronunciation and have students create short sample sentences for 'irritable' and 'classification'.

Instruct students to read the article silently once to grasp the main idea. Ask gist questions: What did ancient Greeks believe controlled personality? Do we still classify personality today? Have students answer the Main Idea MCQ independently, then confirm why option B is correct.

teachingScript.phase: Second reading for detail and evidence
teachingScript.actions: Read the passage aloud or call on student volunteers paragraph by paragraph. Highlight the four humours (yellow bile, black bile, phlegm, blood) and their matching personality traits. Have students complete the Reading Comprehension MCQs and Evidence from the Text section, using 'Check & Compare' to verify textual evidence.

Explicitly teach classification and explanation language: 'according to', 'was linked to', 'was believed to', 'depended on', 'for example', 'even though', 'today, we still'. Demonstrate how these expressions connect historical beliefs to modern habits. Guide students through the short completion practice items.

Direct students to complete the 4 short written-response questions in 2-4 complete sentences each. Walk around the room to provide individualized feedback. Prompt students to click 'Check & Compare' to evaluate their responses against the model answers.

Introduce the final prompt: 'Why do people try to classify personality, and is this useful?' Review the checklist criteria together: 100–140 words, clear stance, reference to the four humours theory, two reasons for classification, target connectors, and a strong concluding sentence. Provide uninterrupted writing time.

Guide students through the Self-check checklist. Instruct them to enter their Name and Student Code, then click 'Submit Lesson'. Point out that submitting reveals the complete model answer for final reflection.

sentences.chunkReading: On the other hand, / an excess of blood / was believed to make / a person / cheerful, energetic, and optimistic.
sentences.directKorean: 반면에, / 피의 과다함은 / 만들 것으로 믿어졌다 / 한 사람을 / 명랑하고, 활기차고, 낙천적으로.
sentences.naturalKorean: 반면에 피가 과다하면 그 사람은 명랑하고 활기차며 낙천적으로 변한다고 믿어졌습니다.

mustKnowChunks.use: 상반되는 두 가지 사실이나 의견을 대조할 때 씁니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: He is quiet; on the other hand, his brother is loud.

mustKnowChunks.use: 어떤 물질이나 양이 기준치를 초과함을 뜻합니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: An excess of sugar is bad for health.

sentences.mustKnowGrammar: 대조 접속어구 'On the other hand'로 시작하며, 주어 'an excess of blood'에 대한 5형식 동사구(was believed to make + obj + adj)가 이어집니다.
sentences.feynmanExplanation: 반대로 피가 왕성하고 넘치면 기분이 항상 좋고 싱글벙글 활력이 넘치는 활발한 사람이 된다고 봤지요.

teachingTranscript.english: 'An excess of blood' means / having too much blood / in the body.
teachingTranscript.korean: 'An excess of blood'는 / 체내에 피가 너무 많음을 의미합니다.

sentences.original: The theory helped people explain why someone might be calm, gloomy, outgoing, or anxious long before modern psychology existed.
sentences.chunkReading: The theory helped people explain / why someone might be / calm, gloomy, outgoing, or anxious / long before modern psychology existed.
sentences.directKorean: 그 이론은 사람들이 설명하도록 도왔다 / 왜 누군가가 ~일 수 있는지 / 침착하거나, 우울하거나, 외향적이거나, 불안한지 / 현대 심리학이 존재하기 훨씬 전에.
sentences.naturalKorean: 이 이론은 현대 심리학이 생겨나기 훨씬 전부터 사람들이 누군가가 왜 침착하거나, 우울하거나, 외향적이거나, 불안한지 설명하는 데 도움을 주었습니다.

mustKnowChunks.example: The map helped us find the way.

sentences.mustKnowGrammar: 'help + 목적어(people) + 원형부정사(explain)' 구문 뒤에 간접의문문 'why + 주어(someone) + 조동사(might) + be...'가 목적어로 쓰였습니다.
sentences.feynmanExplanation: 비록 진짜 과학은 아니었지만, 옛날 사람들에게는 '저 친구는 우울하고, 저 친구는 느긋하네'를 설명해주는 유일한 도구였던 거예요.

teachingTranscript.english: Notice the list of personality adjectives: / calm, gloomy, outgoing, or anxious.
teachingTranscript.korean: 성격 형용사들을 살펴보세요: / 침착한, 우울한, 외향적인, 불안한.

sentences.original: Even though the idea was not scientifically true, it remained popular for a very long time, even into Shakespeare's time.
sentences.chunkReading: Even though the idea / was not scientifically true, / it remained popular / for a very long time, / even into Shakespeare's time.
sentences.directKorean: 비록 그 생각이 / 과학적으로 사실이 아니었을지라도, / 그것은 인기 있는 상태로 남아있었다 / 매우 오랜 시간 동안, / 심지어 셰익스피어의 시대까지도.
sentences.naturalKorean: 그 생각이 과학적으로 진실은 아니었을지라도, 셰익스피어 시대에 이르기까지 아주 오랫동안 널리 사용되었습니다.

mustKnowChunks.example: Even though it rained, we played soccer.

mustKnowChunks.meaning: 인기 있는 상태로 남아있었다, 지속적인 인기를 누렸다
mustKnowChunks.example: The song remained popular for decades.

sentences.mustKnowGrammar: 양보 접속사 'Even though'절과 주절 'it remained popular...'로 이루어진 복문 구조이며, 'even into + 명사'는 연장된 기간을 강조합니다.
sentences.feynmanExplanation: 과학적으로 맞지 않는 이론인데도 무려 2천 년 넘게, 셰익스피어가 연극을 쓸 때까지도 사람들이 믿고 계속 썼어요.

teachingTranscript.english: Shakespeare often used the humours / to describe his characters' moods.
teachingTranscript.korean: 셰익스피어는 등장인물의 기분을 묘사할 때 / 4체액설을 자주 활용했습니다.

sentences.original: Some echoes of this ancient idea still appear today in personality tests, such as the Myers-Briggs test, or in modern traits like extroverted and calm.
sentences.chunkReading: Some echoes of this ancient idea / still appear today / in personality tests, / such as the Myers-Briggs test, / or in modern traits / like extroverted and calm.
sentences.directKorean: 이 고대 아이디어의 일부 메아리(흔적)가 / 오늘날 여전히 나타난다 / 성격 검사에, / 마이어스-브릭스 검사와 같은, / 혹은 현대의 특성들에 / 외향적이거나 침착함과 같은.
sentences.naturalKorean: 이 고대 아이디어의 흔적은 마이어스-브릭스 검사 같은 성격 검사나 '외향적', '침착함'과 같은 현대의 성격 유형 속에 오늘날에도 여전히 남아있습니다.

mustKnowChunks.use: 과거의 관념이 현대까지 영향을 미치고 있음을 비유적으로 표현할 때 사용합니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: We still see echoes of ancient traditions today.
Fruits such as apples and oranges are healthy.

sentences.mustKnowGrammar: 주어 'Some echoes of this ancient idea'에 부사 'still appear today'가 연결되고, 전치사구 'in personality tests... or in modern traits...'가 병렬 연결되어 있습니다.
sentences.feynmanExplanation: 요즘 우리가 흔히 하는 MBTI 성격 검사나 '나 외향적이야' 같은 말 속에도 옛날 4체액설처럼 사람을 몇 가지 유형으로 나누려는 방식이 그대로 들어있어요.

teachingTranscript.english: The word 'echoes' is used metaphorically / to mean lingering influences.
teachingTranscript.korean: 'echoes'라는 단어는 비유적으로 쓰여 / 지속되는 영향력을 의미합니다.

sentences.original: One media psychology expert said classification is our built-in mechanism for organizing information.
sentences.chunkReading: One media psychology expert said / classification is / our built-in mechanism / for organizing information.
sentences.directKorean: 한 미디어 심리학 전문가는 말했다 / 분류는 ~이다 / 우리의 타고난 메커니즘 / 정보를 정리하기 위한.
sentences.naturalKorean: 한 미디어 심리학 전문가는 분류란 정보를 정리하기 위한 인간의 타고난 본능적 메커니즘이라고 말했습니다.

mustKnowChunks.use: 인간이나 시스템에 본능적으로 내재된 기능이나 방식을 뜻합니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Fear is a built-in mechanism for survival.

mustKnowChunks.use: for + 동명사 구문으로 목적이나 용도를 설명합니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Folders are useful for organizing information.

sentences.mustKnowGrammar: 전달 동사 'said' 뒤에 접속사 that이 생략되어 명사절이 오며, 'for + 동명사(organizing)'가 용도를 한정해 줍니다.
sentences.feynmanExplanation: 전문가에 따르면, 인간은 복잡한 세상과 사람들을 몇 개의 서랍(카테고리)으로 딱딱 나누어서 정리해야 마음이 편해지는 타고난 본능이 있대요.

teachingTranscript.english: 'Built-in mechanism' means / a natural, innate way of behaving.
teachingTranscript.korean: 'Built-in mechanism'은 / 자연스럽고 타고난 행동 방식을 의미합니다.

sentenceFrames: People try to classify personality because __________.
According to the ancient Greek theory, personality depended on __________.
For example, too much yellow bile was believed to make a person __________.
Even though this theory was not scientifically true, __________.
Today, people still enjoy personality tests because __________.
Overall, personality classification can be useful, but __________.
paragraphOutline: 1. Topic Sentence: State your stance on why people classify personality.
2. Historical Detail: Mention the ancient Greek four humours theory (yellow bile, blood, etc.).
3. Function / Reason: Explain why people used and still use categories to organize information.
4. Modern Connection: Refer to modern personality tests like Myers-Briggs.
5. Concluding Sentence: Summarize your view on the usefulness and limits of classification.

commonMistakes.mistake: According to ancient Greeks, personality is depend on blood.
commonMistakes.correction: According to ancient Greeks, personality depended on blood.

commonMistakes.mistake: Even though it was not true, but people believed it.
commonMistakes.correction: Even though it was not true, people believed it. (Avoid using 'even though' and 'but' together in one clause).

teacherCorrectionFocus: Ensure students do not use double connectors like 'even though... but'.
Check that the word count is within the target range of 100–140 words.
Verify that students cite at least one specific detail from the text (e.g. four humours or Myers-Briggs).
